memory_update.text: For the Technology theme, use AI infrastructure as the first chokepoint lane: demand starts at AI clusters but investable bottleneck research should move upstream into optics, advanced packaging, HBM test, board power integrity, advanced glass, and qualification gates.

InP substrates are a potential low-attention bottleneck for optical interconnect and CPO; thesis depends on CPO adoption speed, actual InP content, qualified supplier concentration, and capacity expansion timelines.

T-glass and advanced glass fiber appear to be a high-concentration, qualification-heavy substrate materials node; verify the named supplier, share, customer qualification, capacity expansion, and pricing/margin evidence in primary filings.
High-end AI-server MLCCs are not commodity passives; the bottleneck appears to sit in low-ESR/low-ESL, high-capacitance, high-reliability parts used in dense AI accelerator power delivery.
Advanced packaging and memory backend overflow should be tracked as a second-order HBM chokepoint; third-party OSATs may benefit when IDMs allocate internal capacity to high-margin HBM.

2026-2027 advanced-glass capacity expansion is a key catalyst and falsification checkpoint: if added capacity removes pricing power or customers qualify alternatives faster than expected, the bottleneck score should be reduced.
Customer validation for FOPLP, CPO-adjacent packaging, InP substrates, and advanced test/inspection tools is a higher-quality catalyst than generic AI commentary.

Need primary-source verification for all company-specific claims from Substack sources: filings, earnings transcripts, investor presentations, customer announcements, trade press, and capacity disclosures.
Need to identify the unnamed Japanese T-glass supplier in primary sources and map its ticker, segment revenue, AI substrate exposure, capex schedule, and customer concentration.
Need to separate fact from narrative in the AXTI/InP thesis: verify InP revenue mix, six-inch capacity, actual optical/datacom customer exposure, China operating risk, and pricing power.

FORM should remain a high-priority underfollowed HBM test relationship: map it to memory wafer probe and known-good-die validation, then verify HBM probe-card mix, memory customer breadth, share gains, and capacity constraints.

COHU should remain a high-priority underfollowed backend test/inspection relationship: map it to HBM inspection, metrology, contactors, handlers, and AI/HPC thermal test, then verify repeat HBM orders and revenue materiality.

ALAB is best treated as a reference anchor rather than discovery alpha: map it to AI fabric interconnect and PCIe/CXL connectivity silicon, with evidence work focused on concentration, content per cluster, competition, and insourcing risk.

AIXA.DE is an underfollowed upstream optics tools candidate: map it to compound-semiconductor epitaxy equipment for InP/GaAs lasers and photonics, but require order/backlog proof tied specifically to AI optical demand.

AXTI is a speculative-shadow InP substrate candidate: the bottleneck thesis depends on CPO/optical interconnect adoption, actual InP revenue mix, qualification at laser/photonics customers, and proof that concentrated supply creates pricing power.
ONTO maps to advanced packaging inspection/metrology and process control; verify whether AI/HBM/panel-level packaging revenue is large enough to offset broader semiconductor cyclicality.

AMKR is a reference OSAT capacity anchor for advanced packaging and test; keep it in the map but do not upgrade without evidence of direct AI accelerator, HBM-adjacent, 2.5D, fan-out, or interposer work.
KLIC remains a hypothesis around thermocompression bonding and advanced packaging assembly equipment; verify mix shift away from legacy wire bonding and actual HBM/chiplet-related system shipments.

PTI.TW maps to memory backend outsourcing and FOPLP advanced packaging; external context is supportive but primary-source confirmation is required for AMD/Broadcom validation, 90% pilot yield, price increases, and revenue conversion.

Layer 2B still needs primary-source filing checks for all candidates, especially customer concentration, AI/HBM/CPO revenue materiality, backlog conversion, utilization, pricing power, and whether demand is incremental versus cyclical recovery.

Market-pricing checks are still missing for the chunk: current market capitalization, valuation, estimate revisions, short interest, liquidity, and analyst coverage should be collected before Layer 2C or ranking upgrades.

MTSI maps to the optical/signal-integrity node as an underfollowed hypothesis tied to AI data-center interconnect, 800G/1.6T, LPO, and CPO-adjacent components; primary-source design-win and data-center revenue evidence are required.

SMTC maps to the optical-module signal-integrity node as an underfollowed hypothesis; key survival tests are 800G/1.6T design wins, data-center revenue contribution, inventory normalization, and leverage reduction.

TSEM maps to the specialty silicon-photonics foundry node as an underfollowed hypothesis; the thesis survives only if silicon-photonics customer qualifications and AI datacom foundry demand are material.

VRT and ETN are reference anchors for data-center power, cooling, switchgear, UPS, and critical electrical infrastructure; they should benchmark smaller power/cooling discovery names rather than dominate the underfollowed lane.

PWR maps to grid interconnection, transmission, substation, and utility-infrastructure services as an indirect AI data-center deployment bottleneck candidate; evidence must isolate hyperscaler or data-center pull-through from normal utility capex.

POWL maps to switchgear and power-control systems as an underfollowed data-center electrical-equipment hypothesis; the main evidence gap is the share of backlog and revenue tied to AI data centers versus energy and industrial projects.

MOD maps to precision cooling and thermal-management equipment as an underfollowed AI rack-density hypothesis; evidence needed includes data-center cooling revenue, liquid-cooling product mix, and hyperscaler or colocation customer exposure.

CRWD is a reference benchmark for the AI-security control-plane lane; it should be used to judge smaller security automation candidates but requires verification that AI features drive monetization rather than marketing narrative.

S maps to smaller security automation exposure as an underfollowed software hypothesis; survival tests include AI-assisted workflow usage, ARR contribution, retention, enterprise wins, and path to profitability.

The supplied evidence is strongest for the general AI infrastructure chokepoint framework and weaker for ticker-specific exposure across MTSI, SMTC, TSEM, PWR, POWL, MOD, CRWD, and S. Layer 2C should prioritize primary-source filings, earnings transcripts, customer/design-win disclosures, and market-pricing checks.

Current market capitalization, valuation, estimate revisions, liquidity, short interest, and analyst-coverage data remain unverified for this candidate chunk and should not be inferred from the supplied evidence.

Use NVDA as the reference demand anchor for accelerator-led pull-through into HBM, advanced packaging, networking, optics, power integrity, cooling, and data-center infrastructure; do not rank it as an underfollowed discovery candidate.

Use TSM as the reference bottleneck anchor for advanced logic and CoWoS/SoIC-like packaging; smaller OSAT, substrate, test, metrology, and materials candidates should be judged by whether they benefit from TSM capacity constraints or partner outsourcing.
Use AVGO and MRVL as AI fabric and custom-silicon benchmarks for evaluating smaller optical, CPO, DSP, laser, InP substrate, and interconnect candidates.

Keep STX and WDC in the underfollowed lane only as second-order AI storage hypotheses; they are not yet chokepoint candidates unless nearline exabyte growth, pricing, and cloud/AI customer evidence separate them from normal commodity storage cycles.

This candidate chunk is reference-heavy and lacks the strongest underfollowed Layer 2A chokepoint nodes: InP substrates, T-glass, high-end MLCCs, advanced packaging OSAT overflow, probe/test, inspection/metrology, and power-conversion suppliers.
Before promotion to later layers, all six tickers need current market cap, valuation, estimate-revision, liquidity, short-interest, analyst-coverage, and primary-filing evidence checks.

For STX and WDC, the falsification plan should test whether AI/cloud demand is merely coincident with a storage cycle upturn; negative signs include weak nearline exabyte growth, falling pricing, inventory rebuild without end demand, or no cloud customer capex linkage.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. Initial Serenity Layer 2A industry-chain map for the broad Technology theme, narrowed to the most evidence-supported 2026 AI infrastructure chokepoint lanes: optical interconnect/CPO, advanced packaging/HBM overflow, AI-server power integrity components, advanced glass/T-glass substrates, and semiconductor test/inspection/metrology. The map intentionally does not let GPUs, hyperscalers, or other high-attention mega-cap demand leaders dominate the nodes. Instead, it highlights low-attention or indirect suppliers where bottleneck value may hide: InP substrates, T-glass, high-end MLCCs, memory backend OSAT capacity, FOPLP, CPO-adjacent packaging, wafer/package test, inspection, and qualification/certification gates. This is research support only and does not include buy/sell recommendations.

supply_chain_map.node: AI accelerator clusters and hyperscale data-center buildout
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: This is the visible demand engine: AI training and inference clusters drive demand for GPUs/ASICs, HBM, networking, optics, packaging, power delivery, and board-level components. High-attention leaders belong here as demand anchors, not as the main bottleneck discovery target.

Memory bandwidth is a core system constraint for AI compute. HBM growth pulls on upstream wafer test, known-good-die screening, advanced packaging, and backend capacity. The more useful Serenity angle is not only HBM producers, but the tooling and backend nodes that become scarce as HBM ramps.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced packaging capacity: 2.5D, fan-out, FOPLP, chiplet integration, CPO-adjacent packaging
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI accelerators and HBM integration increase packaging complexity and create capacity and yield constraints. Low-attention value may hide in OSATs, bonding tools, panel-level packaging, and companies benefiting from memory-backend overflow.

supply_chain_map.node: Memory backend outsourcing and OSAT overflow
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: If HBM consumes IDM cleanroom, test, and packaging resources, lower-margin conventional DRAM/NAND backend work can be pushed to third-party OSAT providers. This is a second-order bottleneck that may be less crowded than direct HBM names.

supply_chain_map.node: Semiconductor test, inspection, metrology, known-good-die and package-level validation
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: HBM, chiplets, and advanced packages raise the cost of failure. The supply chain needs more wafer probe, package inspection, thermal test, metrology, contactors, handlers, and process-control tools. Bottleneck value may hide in test/inspection suppliers classified as cyclical equipment rather than AI beneficiaries.

supply_chain_map.node: Optical interconnect, silicon photonics, 800G/1.6T transceivers and co-packaged optics
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: As AI clusters scale, moving bits between chips, servers, racks, and data halls becomes a constraint. Optical connectivity can become the next bottleneck after compute and memory, especially if CPO adoption accelerates.

supply_chain_map.node: InP substrates and compound semiconductor wafers
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: High-speed lasers and optoelectronic devices can depend on indium phosphide and related compound semiconductor materials. This node is narrow, specialized, qualification-heavy, and potentially underfollowed because it sits several layers upstream from the AI server.

supply_chain_map.node: Compound semiconductor epitaxy equipment for lasers and photonics
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Optical modules and photonic devices require epitaxial layers. Tool suppliers for compound semiconductor epitaxy may benefit indirectly from AI optical demand, but exposure must be verified through backlog, customer mix, and optical/laser orders.

supply_chain_map.node: T-glass and advanced glass fiber for high-speed substrates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Advanced glass materials used in high-speed electronic substrates can become a hidden AI buildout constraint. The cited source claims one Japanese supplier has roughly 90% share of T-glass, suggesting a concentrated, process-knowledge bottleneck with long qualification cycles.

supply_chain_map.node: AI-server board-level power integrity: high-end MLCCs and low-impedance passive components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI accelerators draw high instantaneous current, requiring dense arrays of high-end capacitors near compute devices. The bottleneck is not commodity MLCCs but a narrow class of high-capacitance, low-ESR, low-ESL parts with limited qualified mass producers.

supply_chain_map.node: 48V rack power, low-voltage conversion and high-density server power delivery
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI racks increase current density and power-conversion complexity. This node may create demand for specialized power modules, inductors, capacitors, connectors, thermal management, and validation equipment. Current evidence in the provided context is strongest for MLCCs, not the entire power chain.

supply_chain_map.node: Customer qualification, certification and design-in gates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Many hidden bottleneck suppliers are protected less by patents and more by long qualification, customer certification, yield learning, and reliability requirements. These gates can slow substitution and make small upstream suppliers strategically important.

supply_chain_map.node: Tier-N supplier visibility, capacity reservation and upstream co-investment
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: The semiconductor bottleneck is shifting from simple chip procurement to control of upstream capacity, yield allocation, and hidden Tier-N suppliers. This raises the value of suppliers that control hard-to-expand capacity even if they are not branded as AI companies.

supply_chain_map.node: High-attention AI chips, GPUs, ASICs and cloud platforms
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: These companies shape demand and bargaining power, but they are not the focus of this Layer 2A map. They should be used as reference anchors to validate downstream pull-through into lower-attention bottleneck nodes.

ticker_relationships.relationship: FormFactor sits at the memory wafer-probe layer where HBM growth can increase demand for advanced DRAM probe cards and known-good-die validation before expensive stacking and packaging steps. The relationship is a chokepoint candidate because probe-card quality, speed, and customer qualification affect HBM yield and ramp cadence.

ticker_relationships.node: HBM inspection, metrology, backend semiconductor test handlers, contactors, AI/HPC thermal test
ticker_relationships.relationship: Cohu maps to the backend test and inspection node where HBM and AI processors raise package complexity, contactor requirements, inspection burden, and thermal-control needs. The candidate relationship depends on whether initial HBM inspection activity converts into repeat orders and material revenue.

ticker_relationships.relationship: Astera Labs is the reference anchor for merchant AI data-center connectivity silicon. Its relationship to the theme is direct: AI clusters need high-speed connectivity among accelerators, CPUs, memory, NICs, switches, and racks. The key question is not thematic fit but durability of customer concentration, content per cluster, and competition.

ticker_relationships.node: Compound semiconductor epitaxy equipment for InP/GaAs lasers and photonic devices
ticker_relationships.relationship: Aixtron sits several steps upstream of AI optical connectivity: AI data centers require optical modules; optical modules require lasers and photonic devices; those require compound-semiconductor epitaxy; Aixtron supplies MOCVD and related epitaxy equipment. This is an underfollowed AI optics derivative because reported demand may be hidden inside broader optoelectronics and power-electronics categories.

ticker_relationships.hidden_signal_to_verify: Actual InP revenue mix, six-inch InP capacity, qualification at laser/photonics customers, China operating risk, margins under volume growth, and whether industry concentration translates into pricing power.
ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Check AXT 10-K/10-Q, earnings transcripts, segment revenue, substrate capacity disclosures, customer qualification commentary, geographic/China risk disclosures, and photonics/laser customer references.
ticker_relationships.node: Indium phosphide substrates and compound semiconductor wafers for optical interconnect and photonics
ticker_relationships.relationship: AXT is a speculative-shadow candidate for the InP substrate layer. The external context frames AXTI as an InP substrate supplier in a near-duopoly with Sumitomo and links InP substrates to high-end optoelectronic devices used in optical interconnect, CPO, and AI data-center networking. The relationship is highly sensitive to CPO adoption speed, InP revenue mix, and customer qualification evidence.

ticker_relationships.hidden_signal_to_verify: Revenue tied specifically to advanced packaging, HBM, panel-level packaging, GPU/TPU/HBM packaging, tool wins at AI packaging customers, and whether packaging intensity offsets broader semiconductor cyclicality.
ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Review Onto Innovation filings, earnings transcripts, product presentations, advanced packaging revenue mix, customer wins, and references to HBM, panel-level packaging, hybrid bonding, and AI packaging.
ticker_relationships.node: Advanced packaging metrology, inspection, lithography, process control, panel-level packaging inspection
ticker_relationships.relationship: Onto Innovation maps to the yield-control layer of advanced packaging and HBM. As heterogeneous integration, panel-level packaging, interconnect density, and HBM/GPU package complexity increase, inspection and metrology intensity can rise. The relationship is plausible but needs revenue attribution to AI packaging rather than general semiconductor process-control cyclicality.

ticker_relationships.hidden_signal_to_verify: Direct AI accelerator, HBM-adjacent, 2.5D, interposer, EMIB, CoWoS-like, fan-out, or memory-backend overflow work; customer concentration; Arizona project milestones; and NVIDIA/AMD/TSMC/Intel-related disclosures.

The relationship is less pure than HBM producers or foundries and requires verification of direct AI accelerator, 2.5D, fan-out, interposer, or HBM-adjacent work.

ticker_relationships.relationship: Kulicke & Soffa maps to the assembly-equipment layer. HBM, chiplets, and heterogeneous-integration packages can require more advanced bonding and assembly steps, potentially creating demand for thermocompression bonding and related advanced packaging systems. The thesis is a hypothesis because legacy wire-bonding cyclicality may still dominate revenue and margins.

This is a potentially underfollowed Taiwan OSAT chokepoint, but customer validation and revenue conversion need primary-source confirmation.
